sections.description: Walks through the patient's baseline health, temporal relationship to semaglutide exposure, and evolution of symptoms that raised suspicion for an immune-mediated necrotising myopathy rather than toxic rhabdomyolysis.
subtopics: Baseline comorbidities and prior liver workup: NAFLD with biopsy-proven steatohepatitis; hypothyroidism with normal TSH; no prior statin or myotoxic supplement exposure
Semaglutide initiation: single 0.25 mg dose with immediate gastrointestinal intolerance, hypovolaemia, and acute kidney injury; early CK 337 U/L
Progressive course over 4 months off drug: proximal limb weakness, dysphagia, dysphonia, loss of postural stability
New atrial fibrillation during initial hospitalization; normal troponin then, later mild hs-troponin and high proBNP
Examination at referral: severe proximal weakness without rash, synovitis, interstitial lung disease signs, or other systemic features
Key labs at deterioration: CK peak 3992 U/L; AST/ALT elevation; inflammatory markers modestly elevated; broad negative autoantibody panel except low-titer isolated SS-B
Clinical red flags for IMNM: subacute progressive symmetric proximal and bulbar weakness with marked CK rise and no cutaneous signs

sections.description: Details the targeted evaluation for proximal weakness with CK elevation, integrates imaging and histopathology, and contrasts competing diagnoses to justify seronegative IMNM.
subtopics: Structured approach to elevated CK and proximal weakness: exclude endocrine, electrolyte, infectious, drug-induced, and primary inflammatory myopathies
Muscle MRI findings: symmetric thigh muscle oedema in proximal vastus lateralis and quadriceps supporting active myopathy

Muscle biopsy interpretation: necrotic and regenerating fibres, CD68+ macrophage myophagocytosis, membrane attack complex on fibres, rare CD3+ cells, overall paucity of lymphocytes consistent with IMNM
Myositis autoantibody panel: negative SRP and HMGCR (plus other MSAs), reinforcing seronegative IMNM subset
Cardiac assessment: echo normal LVEF; CMR with mild regional oedema without late gadolinium enhancement; differential of early myocarditis versus stress cardiomyopathy; resolution on follow-up
Hepatic evaluation: ultrasound and biopsy consistent with NAFLD; persistently abnormal transaminases even after CK normalisation indicating hepatic rather than myopathic source

Key differentials and why less likely: toxic/drug rhabdomyolysis (timing and CK kinetics inconsistent), dermatomyositis/polymyositis (no rash, histology not supportive), inclusion body myositis (pattern and histology discordant), hypothyroid myopathy (TSH normal), steroid myopathy (weakness preceded steroids), neuromuscular junction disorders (CK typically normal)
Synthesis: clinical pattern, MRI, and biopsy converge on seronegative IMNM

sections.section_title: IMNM Pathophysiology and Serology in the Context of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists
sections.description: Provides focused background on immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, its immunopathology and serologic subsets, and explores a plausible link with GLP-1 receptor agonists within current evidence.
subtopics: IMNM definition: aggressive proximal weakness with myofibre necrosis, macrophage-rich myophagocytosis, and limited lymphocytic infiltrates
Immunopathology: complement-mediated injury with membrane attack complex deposition; role of innate immune effector cells
Serologic categories: anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP positivity versus seronegative IMNM (~one-third of cases)
Known triggers: statins (HMGCR association), certain mushrooms/red yeast rice, and other putative exposures
GLP-1 receptor agonists: common adverse effects, emerging signals for lean mass loss and isolated rhabdomyolysis
Distinguishing IMNM from rhabdomyolysis: time course of CK elevation and recovery, need for immunosuppression, biopsy features
Case-specific context: absence of HMGCR/SRP antibodies yet classic histology; rising CK over months after single semaglutide exposure
Hypothesised links to GLP-1 RAs: potential immune triggering in predisposed hosts remains unproven; need for mechanistic and epidemiologic studies

sections.section_title: Management Strategy, Monitoring, and Clinical Course
sections.description: Explains the therapeutic decisions made for severe seronegative IMNM, including the role of corticosteroids and IVIG, supportive care, complication management, and objective markers of response.
subtopics: Initial immunotherapy: pulse methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 5 days followed by prednisone 1 mg/kg/day
Adjunctive therapy: IVIG 2 g/kg over 4 days for severe weakness and bulbar involvement
Response assessment: CK normalisation within weeks, functional improvement, and objective recovery of swallowing and phonation
Complication management: pseudomonal UTI leading to septic shock during taper; CK remained normal, supporting disease control
Steroid tapering and cessation: rapid wean over ~2 months with sustained remission off immunosuppression
Cardiac follow-up: repeat echocardiogram and CMR demonstrating resolution of earlier abnormalities
Supportive measures: swallow safety strategies, physical and occupational therapy, infection risk mitigation while immunosuppressed
Contingency planning for refractory disease: options include re-dosing IVIG and adding steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate, mycophenolate, azathioprine, or rituximab
Drug avoidance and counseling: continued avoidance of GLP-1 receptor agonists and vigilant monitoring if alternative weight-loss strategies are pursued

sections.section_title: Clinical Implications, Causality Assessment, and Practice Points
sections.description: Addresses the likelihood that semaglutide contributed to IMNM, highlights pharmacovigilance principles, and translates lessons into practical guidance for clinicians.
subtopics: Causality framework: application of WHO-Uppsala Monitoring Centre criteria supporting probable association (temporal relationship, dechallenge response, alternative causes unlikely, no ethical rechallenge)
Why not classic drug-induced rhabdomyolysis: absence of immediate severe CK spike and lack of rapid CK normalisation with hydration alone
Practice algorithm for GLP-1 RA users with weakness: prompt CK testing, medication hold, focused history for other myotoxins, MRI-muscle and biopsy if CK remains elevated and weakness progresses
When to suspect IMNM: subacute progressive proximal and bulbar weakness, CK often in the thousands, myopathic MRI, biopsy with necrosis and macrophage infiltration, autoantibodies may be negative
Interpreting transaminases in myopathy: coordinate CK with AST/ALT to localise source; persistently abnormal transaminases after CK normalisation suggest hepatic origin
Monitoring suggestions: consider baseline symptoms review and early CK if myopathic symptoms emerge after GLP-1 RA initiation; educate patients on red flags such as dysphagia and profound fatigue
Reporting and research: encourage adverse event reporting and participation in registries to clarify incidence, mechanisms, and potential predisposing factors
Key takeaways: seronegative IMNM is real and biopsy-driven; early immunotherapy can be decisive; rising use of GLP-1 RAs warrants awareness of rare but serious neuromuscular adverse events
